# Chronological Account of the Agent Failure

## Source material
Anthropic Engineering blog post: ["Effective harnesses for long-running agents"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) (published Nov 26, 2025; authored by Justin Young).

## Setup
Anthropic engineers ran Claude (a frontier coding model — Opus 4.5 is named) on the **Claude Agent SDK**, a general-purpose agent harness with built-in context-management features such as automatic compaction. The harness ran the model in a loop across multiple context windows, so that when one window filled up a new session would pick up where the previous one left off. The framing experiment was a long-running software-engineering task spanning hours/days.

## The task given
A single high-level user prompt of the form: **"build a clone of claude.ai."** No initialization scaffolding, no feature list, no progress log, no `init.sh`, no browser-testing tools were provided up front — just the agent SDK with compaction, given the prompt and left to run.

## What the agent did, in order

### Session 1 (and any single-session attempts) — "one-shotting"
- On receiving the prompt, the agent did **not** decompose the project into small, individually verifiable features. Instead, it "tended to try to do too much at once — essentially to attempt to one-shot the app," attacking the whole production-quality web app in one go.
- It wrote large amounts of code for many features in parallel within the same session.
- Mid-implementation, the agent **ran out of context window**. A feature was left half-built and undocumented at the moment context was exhausted.
- The harness's compaction step ran but, per the article, "doesn't always pass perfectly clear instructions to the next agent" — the summary handed to the successor session was not detailed enough to reconstruct what had been in progress.

### Session 2+ — recovery from a broken handoff
- The next agent woke up to a codebase in an unclear state with a half-implemented feature and no clear notes about what had been attempted.
- It had to **"guess at what had happened, and spend substantial time trying to get the basic app working again,"** burning much of its own context on archaeology and fixes rather than new progress.

### Verification step (when the agent did test things)
- When the agent did try to confirm its work, it relied on **unit tests** and **`curl` commands against a local development server**.
- These passed, and on that basis the agent **marked features as complete** — but, as observed, it "would fail [to] recognize that the feature didn't work end-to-end." The signals it chose to consult did not reach the level of user-facing behavior, so real bugs slipped through and got labeled passing.

### Later sessions — premature victory
- After some features had accumulated in the repo, a fresh agent instance would start, **survey the existing code, see that work had been done, and "declare the job done."** It did this even though the original prompt's full scope had not been satisfied — there was no shared spec against which to check, so partial progress read as completion.

### Each new session — wasted orientation
- Across the loop, every fresh agent began a session **with no memory** of the prior shift. Each one spent tokens re-deriving how to start the dev server, where the project lived, what had been tried, etc. — repetitive overhead that the SDK's compaction did not eliminate.

### Partial improvement when browser automation was added
- The team then gave Claude the **Puppeteer MCP server** and prompted it to test "as a human user would." With browser automation, the agent navigated the app, sent chats, observed responses, and caught bugs that unit tests and `curl` had not surfaced. Screenshots taken by Claude through Puppeteer are shown in the post.
- Even with Puppeteer, one residual failure remained: **Claude could not see browser-native `alert` modals through the Puppeteer MCP**, so features whose flow depended on those modals continued to be buggier than the rest because the agent had no way to perceive them.

## Signals/feedback the agent received
- **Compaction summary** at session boundary — was unreliable/insufficient.
- **Unit tests and `curl` responses** — passed, but did not exercise the user-facing path.
- **The repo state itself** (presence of files/features) — misread as "we're done."
- **Puppeteer screenshots** (after that tool was added) — useful, but blind to native alert modals.

## Where things went wrong (observable failure points)
1. The agent attempted whole-app implementation in one session and exhausted context mid-feature.
2. Compaction-only handoffs did not preserve enough state for the next session to continue cleanly.
3. The next session spent its budget guessing/recovering rather than progressing.
4. The agent used proxy verification (unit tests, `curl`) and concluded features worked end-to-end when they did not.
5. A later session inspected the partial repo and announced the project complete even though many features required by the original prompt were missing.
6. Every new session re-paid the cost of figuring out how to run the project.
7. Even after gaining browser automation, the agent's perception gap (invisible native alert modals) left a class of features under-tested.

## Final outcome (in the as-described, pre-fix experiment)
With only the stock Claude Agent SDK + compaction and the bare "build a clone of claude.ai" prompt, the agent loop **fell short of building a production-quality web app**. The article reports that adding an initializer-agent + coding-agent harness — a JSON feature list (>200 entries for the claude.ai clone, all initially `"passes": false`), a `claude-progress.txt` log, an `init.sh` script, a startup routine (`pwd`, read progress, read feature list, `git log --oneline -20`, run init), git commits with descriptive messages, one-feature-per-session discipline, and Puppeteer-based end-to-end testing — was what enabled reliable multi-session progress. The pre-harness behavior (the failure being analyzed here) is contrasted against that working solution.

Sources:
- [Effective harnesses for long-running agents — Anthropic Engineering](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents)

Engineering at Anthropic
Effective harnesses for long-running agents
Published Nov 26, 2025
Agents still face challenges working across many context windows. We looked to human engineers for inspiration in creating a more effective harness for long-running agents.
As AI agents become more capable, developers are increasingly asking them to take on complex tasks requiring work that spans hours, or even days. However, getting agents to make consistent progress across multiple context windows remains an open problem.
The core challenge of long-running agents is that they must work in discrete sessions, and each new session begins with no memory of what came before. Imagine a software project staffed by engineers working in shifts, where each new engineer arrives with no memory of what happened on the previous shift. Because context windows are limited, and because most complex projects cannot be completed within a single window, agents need a way to bridge the gap between coding sessions.
We developed a two-fold solution to enable the Claude Agent SDK to work effectively across many context windows: an initializer agent that sets up the environment on the first run, and a coding agent that is tasked with making incremental progress in every session, while leaving clear artifacts for the next session. You can find code examples in the accompanying quickstart.
The long-running agent problem
The Claude Agent SDK is a powerful, general-purpose agent harness adept at coding, as well as other tasks that require the model to use tools to gather context, plan, and execute. It has context management capabilities such as compaction, which enables an agent to work on a task without exhausting the context window. Theoretically, given this setup, it should be possible for an agent to continue to do useful work for an arbitrarily long time.
